description: We are SONNE, students in the Computer Technology Engineering (ITC) program at the University of Monterrey (UDEM). We want to participate in this challenge to expand our experience in the engineering and technology industry, and we are very eager to take on the challenge ahead!
summary:
MISSION LAB is a free, open-source 2D pixel-art game in which 1 to 4 players design, launch and operate a CubeSat. Teams balance coupled real-world constraints: mass, volume, solar power, eclipse battery drain, orbital mechanics, launch-vehicle routes and ground-station data budgets. They must pass a 13-point GO/NO-GO Flight Readiness Review, then fly real Earth-observation missions, Amazon Fire Alarm and Greenland Ice Watch, from Mission Control, where their command sequence is scored against an optimal autopilot.

It answers the challenge by turning authentic NASA systems engineering, grounded in CubeSat 101, Keplerian orbits, VIIRS and Landsat, into a hands-on game anyone can play.

It matters because the challenge is genuine. Scores reflect real systems-engineering skill, so we propose a global leaderboard as a merit-based talent pipeline, helping NASA find high-potential students worldwide and connect them with scholarships, regardless of résumé or background.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO / HOW DOES IT WORK?

Mission Lab is a free, open-source 2D pixel-art game in which 1 to 4 players work together as a CubeSat mission team: Scientist, Engineer, Launch Lead and Ground Control. A playthrough follows five phases, as a real mission does:

1. Briefing: the science question, a real map of the target area, budget, launch date, real NASA science notes and the success criteria for the Bronze, Silver and Gold medals.

2. Build & Review: players build a 2U, 3U or 6U CubeSat in a shared hangar. The budgets are coupled: mass, volume, solar power, battery depth of discharge during eclipse, daily data downlink (GB/day), cost and schedule. Players also resolve problems that come up during testing and use three consoles: an Orbit Map with real ground tracks and day/night, a Rocket Console that runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on a weighted graph of launch routes, and a Ground Station Desk with antenna coverage, data budget and battery charts. Launch is allowed only after the design passes a 13-point GO/NO-GO Flight Readiness Review.

3. Launch: countdown, liftoff, orbit insertion, solar array deployment and first contact.

4. Mission Control: one simulated day in orbit. Players queue IMAGE commands for passes over the target and DOWNLINK commands for ground-station contacts such as Svalbard and Fairbanks. To score fairly, an optimal autopilot flies the same spacecraft on the same day, and the team is compared against it.

5. Results: the image the satellite captured, a score out of 100 and a medal.

There are two missions: Amazon Fire Alarm (night-time thermal-infrared fire detection, modeled on VIIRS) and Greenland Ice Watch (daytime high-resolution glacier monitoring, modeled on Landsat 8/9).

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

Players learn real systems engineering by doing it: every choice affects other budgets, as on a real spacecraft. The game is free, runs offline on ordinary computers and needs no prior knowledge. The co-op roles teach teamwork across engineering disciplines.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

Beyond education, we propose Mission Lab as an open, merit-based way for NASA and its partners to discover talent. The constraints are genuinely hard: in Mission 2, out of 4,860 possible designs, only 23 achieve Full Success and 13 (0.27%) reach Exemplary. A high score therefore demonstrates real systems-engineering skill. Our proposed next step is a global leaderboard that connects top players with scholarships, mentorship and internships, regardless of résumé, geography or economic background.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

Java 17, the libGDX framework and LWJGL3 (with full-window scaling, including macOS Retina displays); Gradle; JUnit 5 with 91 automated tests, plus a separate balance checker that scores every possible design; our own data structures (a directed weighted graph with Dijkstra's algorithm, and FIFO queues); pixel art drawn in code and pixel fonts under the SIL Open Font License, so the game needs no external art files; Git/GitHub; and the AI assistants Claude and Gemini (see the disclosure below). It runs on any Windows, macOS or Linux desktop or laptop.

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

It turns real aerospace trade-offs into a co-op game for players sharing one screen. Players don't just read about orbits, power budgets or launch logistics: they make the decisions and live with the results. Benchmarking each team against an optimal autopilot makes scores fair across different spacecraft, and linking scores to real opportunities turns a game into a way to discover engineering talent.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Scientific accuracy: NASA's CubeSat 101, the Cal Poly CubeSat Design Specification (2 kg per U), the FCC's five-year rule for deorbiting satellites in low Earth orbit, Keplerian orbital mechanics, and the geometry of polar ground stations such as KSAT Svalbard.

- Fair balance: an automated checker confirms that several different designs can win and that every part is useful.

- Accessibility: open source, lightweight, runs offline and uses no external assets.

- Simplification: the numbers are simplified for teaching while keeping realistic orders of magnitude.

- Branding: we followed NASA's branding rules; the game uses no NASA logos or insignia.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

Team SONNE used AI assistants (Claude and Gemini) for brainstorming, research, coding and debugging, testing, translation and drafting this submission. Every AI contribution was reviewed and verified by the team; the code was checked with the automated tests and the balance checker. No AI or machine learning runs inside the game, and no AI-generated content uses NASA logos or branding. This disclosure is also included in the project's README.
